summary: Gives recommendations for randomizing transport-protocol port numbers to defend against blind attacks on TCP and similar protocols. Such attacks rely on guessing the connection five-tuple, and randomizing the ephemeral port makes this harder.

plainLanguage.summary: An attacker who can guess the doorway number of a conversation can cause trouble. Picking the number unpredictably makes guessing hard.

questions: how do hosts pick random source ports
what port range should ephemeral ports use
subtitle: Five ways for a host to pick unpredictable client port numbers, so blind attackers cannot guess which connection to hit.

tldr.problem: Blind attacks on TCP and similar protocols only work if the attacker can guess the five-tuple that identifies a connection. Hosts that pick client ports in a simple counting sequence make the one unknown part easy to guess.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five local algorithms for choosing the ephemeral (client) port, from plain random choice to hash-based and random-increment schemes, and advises using the whole 1024-65535 range.
tldr.outcome: The algorithms are local policies that can be deployed one host at a time without breaking any transport protocol. They raise the bar against off-path attackers but do not replace cryptographic protection.

facts.label: Collision rate in the cited study

today: RFC 6056 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its appendix surveys the algorithms used by FreeBSD, Linux, NetBSD, OpenBSD and OpenSolaris at the time of writing in 2011.

sections.title: Why Port Numbers Need to Be Hard to Guess
sections.content:
Several blind attacks work against TCP and similar protocols without the attacker ever seeing the victim's packets. The RFC says the consequences range from throughput reduction to broken connections or data corruption. All of them rely on the attacker being able to guess or know the five-tuple that identifies the connection: protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

Most of that tuple is public. Servers sit on well-known ports, and the client address is often known. What is left is the client's ephemeral port, the port the networking stack picks automatically when an application does not ask for a specific one. If the attacker cannot guess it, an off-path attack becomes much harder.

The RFC is clear about its limits. These algorithms are not a replacement for cryptographic protection such as IPsec, the TCP MD5 option or the TCP Authentication Option, and they give no help when the attacker can sniff the connection's packets. Their selling point is improved resistance to off-path attacks with very little effort and no key management. They are local modifications that can be deployed incrementally and do not violate the specifications of TCP, UDP, UDP-Lite, SCTP, DCCP or RTP (when the RTP application explicitly signals its RTP and RTCP ports).
sections.plainLanguage: Your chat with a friend is identified by a few numbers, and only your own door number is a secret. If the bully cannot guess it, he cannot butt in.

sections.title: Ephemeral Ports and the Traditional Algorithm
sections.content:
IANA reserves the 16-bit TCP and UDP port space in three parts: well-known ports 0 through 1023, registered ports 1024 through 49151, and dynamic or private ports 49152 through 65535. The dynamic range is meant for ephemeral ports.

Whatever port is chosen, the resulting five-tuple has to be unique. The traditional BSD approach keeps one global next_ephemeral counter per protocol, hands out the next port, wraps at the end of the range and skips ports that fail a check_suitable_port() test. It works adequately when few connections outlive a full pass through the range.

Its weakness is that the counter is shared by all connections, so the next port is easy to predict. An attacker who runs an innocent-looking server that the client connects to gets a reference value. If the attacker can make the client connect periodically, subtracting consecutive source ports reveals how many outgoing connections the host made in that time.
sections.plainLanguage: If every new chat just takes the next number in line, anyone who sees your last number knows your next one, and can even count how many chats you started.

sections.title: What a Good Algorithm Needs
sections.content:
The RFC lists three goals: make future ports hard to predict, minimize collisions of instance-ids (five-tuples), and avoid clashing with applications that depend on specific port numbers.

Collisions matter because a five-tuple that is free locally may still be in use at the remote system. If a web server did the active close, the old tuple stays in TIME-WAIT there for 2*MSL. Reusing it can cause connection failures or TIME-WAIT assassination, with a risk of data corruption. Picking purely random ports can reuse them too quickly, while counting upward avoids reuse but is trivially predictable. The algorithms below are compromises between those two.

Other rules follow. Ports in use by a TCP in the LISTEN state should not be used as ephemeral ports, because an attacker could otherwise steal an incoming connection, either through a TCP simultaneous open or by binding a more specific socket. Because of how the sockets API does passive opens, implementations should also avoid ports in the CLOSED state. SCTP is not affected by this issue, and DCCP is affected only by the more-specific-socket vector.

On the range, selection algorithms should use the whole range 1024-65535, and SHOULD use the largest possible range, since that lowers an off-path attacker's chances. Ports needed for local services SHOULD NOT be in the pool, so administrators should exclude only the registered ports of services the host actually offers, rather than all of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick your door number so it is hard to guess, but do not reuse one that was just used, and never take a door another program is waiting behind. A bigger building has more doors to guess from.

sections.title: The Five Algorithms
sections.content:
Ephemeral port selection algorithms SHOULD obfuscate their choices. The RFC gives five, all built around a check_suitable_port() test and a retry loop.

  • Algorithm 1, simple randomization: start at a random port in the range and scan upward until a suitable one is found. It hides the global connection count, but it is biased toward the first available port after a run of unavailable ones. If the exclusion list is large, an attacker gets a noticeably better guess.
  • Algorithm 2, re-randomize on collision: pick a new random port each time instead of scanning. It can fail with very small probability even when ports remain. The RFC cites measurements showing one choice is usually enough and two almost always suffice.
  • Algorithm 3, simple hash-based: an offset function F() of the local IP, remote IP, remote port and a secret key gives each destination its own starting point in the range, and a counter moves upward from there. This gets the low port reuse of the BSD scheme while keeping unpredictability. F() should be a cryptographic hash such as MD5. A global counter still leaks the host's connection count to an attacker who can observe consecutive ports.
  • Algorithm 4, double hash: adds a table of TABLE_LENGTH counters, picked by a second hash G(), so increments are separated into many spaces. Port reuse is probabilistically lower than in Algorithm 3 and traffic analysis is much harder. The cited study found a TABLE_LENGTH of 10 already improves on Algorithm 3. The cost is extra CPU for G() and kernel memory for the table.
  • Algorithm 5, random increments: a counter advances by a random amount from 1 to N each time. Small N behaves like the BSD counter and large N behaves like Algorithm 1. The RFC's pseudo-code uses 500 and says the value should be configurable so administrators can pick their own trade-off.

The RFC stresses that the goal is to make guessing harder, not to produce mathematically random sequences. It also notes that random() output must be unpredictable, and that typical POSIX implementations do not necessarily meet that.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tricks pick the door number completely at random, some start at a secret spot for each friend, and some take random-sized steps along the hallway. They mix surprise with not bumping into doors used recently.

sections.title: Secret Keys for the Hash-Based Algorithms
sections.content:
Algorithms 3 and 4 are only as strong as their secret key. An attacker who knows which hash function is used and can collect enough of the victim's ephemeral ports may simply search the whole key space. The RFC says key lengths of 128 bits should be adequate, and that the key should be as random as possible, following the randomness advice in RFC 4086.

The key can also be changed over time, but changing it makes every destination's offset jump, so a port recently used toward the same endpoint may be selected and collisions may occur. The change should be made with care, for example when the system boots, when a time has expired, when the key has been used so often it should be regarded as insecure, when few transport instances are active, when system load is low, or when enough real random data is available. Pseudo-random key changes should not be done.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret is like the code behind a lock. A longer code is harder to crack, and changing it now and then helps, but only when changing it will not cause a mix-up.

sections.title: Choosing an Algorithm
sections.content:
An empirical study cited by the RFC found that every algorithm in the document keeps collision rates low, at most 0.3% in the scenarios tested, though results may vary with traffic and network setup. Algorithms 1 and 2 showed the largest collision rates of the five.

The trade-offs are summarized as follows. The traditional counter is simple and has low port reuse but is trivially predictable. Algorithms 1 and 2 give real randomization but more collisions. Algorithm 3 separates destinations well but costs a hash computation. Algorithm 4 improves on 3 at the expense of more processor cycles and extra memory. Algorithm 5 is a middle ground controlled by N.

One special case can rule out Algorithms 3 and 4. Some applications call bind() with port zero before connecting, and in some BSD-derived systems that selects an ephemeral port before the remote address and port are known, so the hash cannot be computed. Implementations should consider Algorithm 2 in that case, or use lazy binding, which delays port selection until connect() or send(). The RFC says Linux implements lazy binding.
sections.plainLanguage: No single trick is best. Some are quick but a bit guessable, some are very secret but take more work, so you pick the one that fits your computer.

sections.title: Interaction with NAPT
sections.content:
A Network Address Port Translator rewrites both addresses and ports, so from outside the network the port a client appears to use is chosen by the NAPT, not the client. NAPTs should therefore consider using these algorithms too.

The rules are: a NAPT that does not preserve ports SHOULD obfuscate the port whenever it changes it; a NAPT that does preserve ports SHOULD obfuscate only when the port must change because it is already in use; and a NAPT that preserves parity and must change a port SHOULD obfuscate it, for example by forcing the lowest-order bit to the wanted parity.

Some applications expect contiguous ports. Random algorithms such as 1, 2 and 5 are likely to break that expectation, while Algorithms 3 and 4 select consecutive ports so they stay contiguous unless a needed port is taken. Since deployed NAPTs use many different selection methods, any application depending on a specific one is likely to suffer interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A building's front desk may hand out its own door numbers for you. So the front desk should pick them unpredictably too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Obfuscating ports is no replacement for cryptographic mechanisms such as IPsec. An eavesdropper who can see the connection learns addresses, ports and sequence numbers and can attack easily, and port obfuscation gives no extra protection there.

The RFC recommends the whole range 1024-65535 but also a local list of unavailable ports. If that list is significant, Algorithm 1 may be highly biased and generate predictable ports. If the IANA Registered Ports list is accepted unchanged, certain ports could have 500 times the probability of others, so systems with large unavailable lists MUST NOT use Algorithm 1.

For Algorithms 3 and 4, an F() that gives identical offsets for different inputs more often than chance reduces the effect. An attacker using a dynamically assigned IP address can sample the current offset and later use it against an innocent peer that gets the same address, but only until the key changes, and both parties would need to act as servers, which the RFC says is not very common.
sections.plainLanguage: Hiding your door number does not help if the bully is already standing in the hallway watching you. For that you need a real lock.
